q: The two Brisbane immigration files
known: Paper only, held in Brisbane, not digitised. Case files of this era normally carry the sponsor, the addresses, the occupations, and often photographs. 1972/4964 is already marked Open.
settles: Anyone can order a copy through the National Archives of Australia.

q: The restricted Caserta images
known: Some record images return “This record can only be displayed on certain accounts.” The index and the machine transcriptions are open; the scans are not.
settles: A visit to a FamilySearch centre or an affiliate library unlocks them.

q: The two un-scanned volumes
known: Arpaia births 1895 and Forchia births 1897 are not digitised. This was first inferred from ark arithmetic — the shelf-marks run consecutively and skip those years — and it is now CONFIRMED FROM THE HOLDINGS LIST ITSELF: Antenati's Forchia births run …1895, 1896, 1898, 1899… with no 1897 in any fondo or either archive. Between them the two volumes hold Angelo Zampiello's birth and Filomena Annecchino's, the two this archive cannot prove.
settles: Ordering or reading those two volumes at Benevento. See the Antenati page.

q: The processetti
known: Marriage supplement files: birth extracts, parental consents, and death certificates of parents already dead. One file can carry two generations backwards. None have been read.
settles: Time, and a reader of Italian record hands. This is the largest unworked seam in the project.

q: The Museo Alfonsiano, Arienzo
rank: The old bishop's palace beside Sant'Andrea
known: It stands next to the church in which this family was baptised for two centuries, and may hold or know of parish material that was never filmed.
settles: A letter, or a visit.

q: DNA
known: Matches on the Falco and Zampiello sides could confirm or break the Annecchino descent below, and could find living cousins in Campania. No register can do that.
settles: The family already has tests in play; the matches need working through.

q: TWO sons called Giovanni, alive at the same time
known: Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida have TWO sons of this name on the books, and the civil birth act read on 14 September 2026 makes them impossible to merge. The parish burial of 27 November 1841 reads «JOANNES FALCO FILIUS JOSEPHI ET ANTONIAE DI GUIDA, aetatis suae ANNORUM 24 CIRCITER» — born about 1817. DON GIOVANNI FALCO the deacon was born 6 APRIL 1825, now fixed by his civil act AND his parish baptism on the same day, and died 26 November 1849. The 1841 man cannot be the deacon, who outlived him by eight years; and the deacon cannot be the 1841 man, who would have been sixteen, not twenty-four. So the household had TWO LIVING SONS NAMED GIOVANNI for sixteen years — which cuts against everything this archive has learned about the necronym, where a name is given AGAIN only after the first child carrying it has died. THE ARCHIVE HAD NOT NOTICED THIS. Both records sat in it, in different files, neither ever read against the other.
settles: ANSWERED 15 September 2026 — AND THE ANSWER IS THE ONE THIS PAGE CALLED UNLIKELY. The 1841 burial has now been READ FROM THE IMAGE: «Anno Domini 1841 die vero 27. Novembris obiit JOANNES FALCO filius JOSEPHI et ANTONIAE DI GUIDA, aetate sua ANNORUM 24 CIRCITER … cujus cadaver in Sodalitate S. Mariae Gratiarum jacet», the margin reading GIOVANNI FALCO. The machine transcript was accurate, the age is confirmed, and this man was born about 1817 — so he is NOT the deacon, whose birth on 6 April 1825 is fixed by two independent registers. THE HOUSEHOLD REALLY DID HAVE TWO LIVING SONS NAMED GIOVANNI, for sixteen years, and the necronym rule does not explain it: the elder was alive and eight years old when his brother was christened. WHAT IS STILL UNEXPLAINED: **THIS PARAGRAPH SAID THE OPPOSITE UNTIL 16 SEPTEMBER 2026, AND IT WAS WRONG.** It read: «*the register runs from a child buried 26 November straight to a tailor of eighty buried 7 December, so the days on either side of the 27th are accounted for … it is now more likely that the 1841 transcript is wrong*». **The days either side are NOT accounted for.** Those two acts are numbers 86 and 87 and the deaths they record are **26 November and 7 December** — **eleven days in which the comune registered nothing at all**, with the Falco burial of the 27th inside them. The register does it twice: acts 80 and 81 are deaths of **30 October and 13 November**, a fortnight, in a volume that otherwise enters a death every two or three days in that season. **The civil register was not capturing every death at Arienzo**, so its silence is no evidence against the parish book. (The volume also ends at act **91**, not ninety.) **So the last thing this entry called unexplained is explained: the civil register simply did not record that fortnight. The two-Giovanni reading stands, and nothing now argues against it.** What remains is to read the 1841 burial from the image — it is held only as a machine transcript, and «24 circiter» is the kind of number this register guesses. Then look for an elder Giovanni's baptism about 1817, which would settle it either way: if he exists, there were two; if the 1817 baptism is not there, the 1841 age is wrong and there was only ever one.

q: Where is Matteo Falco's death? — NOW SEVEN YEARS
known: This is the most answerable it has ever been. Both his children's marriage acts — Gioacchino's of 16 May 1796 and Giuseppe's of 4 August 1802 — call them «filium Matthei, et Franciscae Crisci» with NO «quondam» before either parent, and this scribe uses «quondam»: on the 1802 leaf itself he writes «filium quondam Caroli Antonii, et Emiliae», father dead and mother living. So Matteo and Francesca were BOTH ALIVE ON 4 AUGUST 1802. The 1814 act calls his son «del fu Matteo», and all six civil death indexes from 1809 to 1814 have been read page for page with no Falco of his generation in them. It is an argument from silence, published as strong evidence and not as proof.
settles: The Arienzo parish death register, 1802–1809. Seven years, one register, one parish — and the same seven years hold Francesca Crisci.

q: Is the widow of 1805 his wife? — ONE WORD
known: «FRANCISCA CRISCI, VIDUA […] FALCO», buried in the confraternity of Santa Maria delle Grazie. If she is the founder's wife, then Matteo died between August 1802 and December 1805 and the window above closes to three and a half years. The machine renders the word after «vidua» as «Manel». It could be MATTHEI. Everything turns on it, and the image has not been read — the attempt hit a rate limit.
settles: One image, at magnification.

q: Who was Matteo Falco's father?
known: Matteo was an adult by 1759 and fathering children from 1767 to 1786. His own marriage — which would name his father — should sit in the Arienzo parish marriage register between about 1760 and 1766. A 2,056-page sweep failed to find it, but that sweep WAS SEARCHING THE WRONG COLLECTION: the marriage register is a separate FamilySearch set, and the re-run on the right one returned 1,260 Falco pages and forty alphabetical marriage-index leaves. None of those indexes covers the 1760s yet.
settles: Find a marriage index covering the 1750s and 1760s. That is the only instrument that can turn «not found» into «not there».

q: Did Gioacchino really marry at seventeen?
known: The act names him «JOACHIM FALCO FILIUM MATTHEI, ET FRANCISCAE CRISCI», so he is unambiguously the founder's son, and his surviving baptism is 2 February 1779 — seventeen years and three months before the wedding, and eighteen when his daughter Giovanna was baptised in May 1797. The alternative, that he is the FIRST Joachim of 25 November 1774 and was twenty-one, is closed by that entry's own margin: a drawn cross and «obiit die 11 Decembris 1777», corroborated by a burial in the parish death register. Seventeen is young, and the archive records that it is young.
settles: ANSWERED 14 September 2026. The 1779 baptism is READ FROM THE IMAGE, on a SECOND FILMING of the page (3Q9M-CSD3-13HT-V, found beside it in a sweep): «Anno D[omi]ni Millesimo Septingentesimo Septuagesimo nono 1779, die vero SECUNDA 2 FEBRUARII, R[everendu]s D[ominu]s D. JOSEPH MIGLIORE Substitutus baptizavit infantem natum ex MATTHEO FALCO, et FRANCISCA CRISCI conjugibus hujus Parochiae, qui nominatus est JOACHIM; Commater fuit DOROTHEA D'ADDIO, Obstetrix vero CECILIA MARTONE». Two independent films, two independent machine transcripts and one image reading now agree. Seventeen stands, and it is still young.

q: When did Giuseppe Falco die?
known: The founder's son was alive and named as a living father in November 1849 and again in April 1854, at about seventy-four. FIFTEEN CONSECUTIVE YEARS of Arienzo death registers, 1844 to 1858, have now been read out — two of them act by act, because they have no index at all — and he is in none of them.
settles: 1859 onward, and then the post-1865 Italian series, which unlike the Bourbon one IS full-text searchable.

q: What became of TWO daughters? — ANSWERED, BOTH OF THEM
known: GIOVANNA and FRANCESCA MARIA LUCIA, daughters of Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida, are baptised and neither appears in the Arienzo death registers of 1844–1858. They married, died before 1844, or left. THIS QUESTION USED TO NAME THREE DAUGHTERS, and the third was MADDALENA — whose fate this archive had already settled on another page and never carried back to here. She died on 31 May 1825, a week short of her seventh birthday, and her act is in the 1825 register this archive read out act by act. Reading her BAPTISM from the image on 14 September 2026 is what exposed the contradiction: the question was stale, not open.
settles: ANSWERED IN FULL, 14 September 2026, both halves in one day. FRANCESCA MARIA LUCIA married RAFFAELE CRISCI on 5 JANUARY 1839 — atto 1 of the year, «FALCO FRANCESCA | Falco Giuseppe, [Gui]da Antonia». She was twenty-six. And GIOVANNA: the Arienzo marriage tavola for 1829 has her at atto 10 — «FALCO GIOVANNA | Falco Giuseppe, e Guida Antonia», married ANIELLO CRISCI on 6 September 1829, at twenty-four. She married into the family next door. BOTH MARRIED CRISCI — and so did their brother Matteo in 1834, and their cousin Anna Falco in 1818. Four Falco–Crisci marriages in twenty-one years, between two households on one street, none of it visible until the marriage indexes were opened.

q: Is Francesco Falco of Paolisi an ancestor?
known: The earliest Arienzo Falco household with a stated origin. The dates would allow him to be Matteo's grandfather. No document joins them, and this archive has not joined them.
settles: The 1672–1738 baptism register, read properly.

q: Filomena Annecchino's act of birth — WHY IT IS NOT FOUND
known: The descent from Carmine Annecchino and Maria Carfora fits the tree exactly — including the grandfather's name — but her own birth record has never been found. This archive blamed FamilySearch's paging limit and fuzzy matching across Annecchino, Annecchini and Anicchino. ANTENATI DOES NOT HOLD THE VOLUME. Its holdings list, enumerated on 13 September 2026, gives Forchia 500 registers across TWO archives — Caserta and Benevento — and three fondi. The births run 1809–1865 and then, in the «Stato civile italiano» fondo at Benevento, 1866, 1867, 1868 … 1894, 1895, 1896, 1898, 1899, 1900 … THERE IS NO 1897, in any fondo or either archive. Forchia's birth INDEXES stop at 1849 and its PROCESSETTI stop at 1865, so neither of those reaches her either.
settles:
NOW TESTED, and the answer is not the one this page gave twice today. FamilySearch's «Benevento Civil Registration (State Archive) 1810–1942» (collection 2475030) DOES cover Forchia in 1897 — a control search on IULIANO, a common Forchia surname, returns about thirty Forchia records in every year from 1894 to 1899, 1897 included. So the year and the town are both indexed. AND SHE IS STILL NOT THERE. Searching the collection for CARMINE ANNECCHINO as father and MARIA CARFORA as mother returns their children at Forchia — Giacinta 1883, Agata 1884, Giacomo 1887, Agata 1889, Lucia and Alfonso both 2 Aug 1892, Alfonso Carmine 1894, Giacomo 1901 — WITH NO CHILD OF 1897 AMONG THEM. Searching by name for a Filomena Annecchino born 1895–1899 returns nothing at all; the only two «Maria Filomena Annecchino» in the whole collection are of 1864 (daughter of Sabatino and Mariantonia Carfora) and 1878 (daughter of Carmine and GIOVANNA CRISCI — the other Carmine).

SO THE EXPLANATION IS NEITHER PAGING NOR FUZZY MATCHING. THE SECOND POSSIBILITY IS NOW CLOSED, and it was closed by a record this archive already held. This entry used to end: «OR — and this archive has not been willing to say it before — SHE WAS NOT BORN AT FORCHIA IN 1897.» That is refused by her own Queensland death registration, 1988/6856, which has sat in data/qld-bdm.tsv marked «ours»: it gives her birth year as 1897 and names her father as CARMINE ANECHINO — the descent this archive reconstructed from Italian records, arriving from an Australian civil source that never touched them. Her Find a Grave memorial adds the birthplace in words, «1897, Forchia, Provincia di Caserta». SO THE BIRTH IS NOT IN DOUBT; THE ACT IS MISSING. Antenati has no Forchia 1897 birth volume in any fondo, so only FamilySearch could hold it, unindexed or misindexed — and every one of her siblings is indexed while she is not. THIS QUESTION WAS STALE FOR MONTHS: the file that answers it and the page that asked it sat in the same repository, which is the failure this archive now watches for above all others. The remaining move is the volume itself at the Archivio di Stato di Benevento, and her MARRIAGE to Carminantonio, which would state her age and birthplace on a record's authority.

q: Was the cross for gallantry?
known: The war itself is settled: the family's own papers hold the Croce al Merito di Guerra conferred on «all'operaio Zampiello Angelo di Tommaso» for operations in East Africa from 3 October 1935. What is NOT settled is the family's account that it was for saving many lives. A merit cross is given for service in a theatre; gallantry would ordinarily carry a Medaglia al Valor Militare instead. The bravery may be true and separately awarded, or it may be the family's gloss on this certificate.
settles: His foglio matricolare at the Archivio di Stato di Benevento — which would also give the First World War service of a man born in 1895, entirely untraced.

q: Angelo Zampiello's birth record
known: His birth date is now corroborated by his memorial card, but the Arpaia births of 1895 are one of the two volumes not digitised, so the act itself is still unread.
settles: Ordering the volume at the Archivio di Stato di Benevento. See the Antenati page.

q: When did Carmine and Francesca arrive? — ANSWERED
known: The passenger list has now been pulled and read. NAA item 12100311 is the FREMANTLE disembarkation return for the ss SYDNEY of the Lauro Lines — and the Falco are NOT in it; that list runs DE CAIRES … D'ITRI … MARTINO and holds no F at all. They are in the Quarantine Service list bound in behind it, which covers the whole ship for every port. At numbers 492 onward: «FALCO Carmine — Tourist — Naples — BRISBANE — 43 Mount Joy, Petrie Terrace, Brisbane — 2.9.63», and FALCO Francesca on the line below. The address was notified on 2 September 1963, nearly seven months before they sailed. The ship is the Sydney, official number 668, master Leopoldo Cafiero, Genoa to Brisbane, arrived 26.3.64.
settles: Closed, and it CORRECTS this archive. The direct line said Carmine and Francesca reached Brisbane «about 1957» — an inference from the 1957–1977 span of their Brisbane immigration file, never a record. The arrival is 26 MARCH 1964. The 1957 end of the file's date range still wants an explanation; it may be when the file was opened rather than when anyone arrived. CARMINANTONIO and FILOMENA, the generation above, were still untraced when this was written — they are now found, in the question below.

q: When did Carminantonio and Filomena arrive? — ANSWERED
known: Found on FindMyPast's copy of the Australian national passenger lists on 13 September 2026, from inside the paywall. FILOMENA FALCO arrived 5 FEBRUARY 1968 — NAA barcode 9788535, page 251. CARMINANTONIO FALCO arrived 19 MAY 1969 — NAA barcode 12211391, page 1711. A second crossing under the spelling «Carminatonio» arrived 24 JULY 1972 — barcode 12047001, page 1605. Set beside the son's arrival of 26 March 1964 the shape is chain migration, and the archive now has the dates for it: the son crossed first, his mother followed nearly four years later, and his father sixteen months after her.
settles: STILL OPEN, and it matters: the transcripts give a name, a year and an arrival date, and NOTHING ELSE — no age, no ship, no port. The identification rests on the forename, which is not one that turns up twice, and on the dates falling exactly where the family's own account puts them. The NAA images are the proof and none of the three has been pulled. They are free, at recordsearch.naa.gov.au, by barcode and page — which is precisely how the 1964 voyage was proved, and that one turned out to be bound in a list nobody would have predicted.

q: Two Carmine Annecchinos
known: One with a wife Maria Carfora, one with Maria Giovanna Crisci — and children twelve days apart in September 1883. Two men, or an indexing error.
settles: The Forchia baptisms, read directly.

q: Which Raffaele is generation four? — ANSWERED
known: Vincenzo Falco and Andreana Crisci named a son RAFFAELE twice: act 56 of 25 April 1816, and act 47 of 10 May 1818, both born in their own house on strada Camellara. Ordinarily the first of two children sharing a name has died before the second is named — but no burial had been found, so this archive carried generation four as DISPUTED rather than assert the likelier answer. The 1817 death register settles it. On 28 OCTOBER 1817, «Raffaele Falco figlio di Vincenzo Falco, e d'Andreana Crisci» was declared dead at seven in the morning, aged about eighteen months. That is the child of April 1816. The Raffaele of 10 May 1818 is the one who lived, married Angela Rosa Morgillo and died in 1880. Generation four is documented.
settles: Closed — and it closed something else on the way. The burial was declared by GIUSEPPE FALCO, 37, massaro di campagna of strada Camellara, who with Sabato Vassallo is recorded as a «PARENTE» of the family. Giuseppe is a documented son of Matteo, which would make him this child's great-uncle. It is the second time the Arienzo registers use the word kin of a Falco declarant on that street. And the age problem the two birth acts left behind — Vincenzo thirty-five in 1816 and twenty-seven in 1818 — IS NOW SOLVED. His baptism extract, found in his marriage dossier, has him baptised on 1 FEBRUARY 1792. He was twenty-six in May 1818, so the 1818 act's twenty-seven is right by the reckoning these clerks used, counting the year a man is in. He was twenty-four in 1816, so the 1816 act's thirty-five is simply an error. The extract also explains the name: he was christened VINCENZO RAFFAELE, and was passing on his own second name to both sons.

q: Arcangelo Crisci, twice — ANSWERED
known: He appeared both as Andreana Crisci's father and as the husband of Anna Falco: one man twice married, or two men? The 1817 birth register settles it — TWO Arcangelo Crisci declare births in that single year, one aged 52 and one aged 30. And the 1820 death register now says who Anna Falco was. She died on 23 August 1820, aged twenty-five, «moglie di ARCANGELO CRISCI … FIGLIA DI PASQUALE FALCO … E DI CHIARA RIVETTI» — a daughter of this line's own generation two, and a sister of Vincenzo. Seven months earlier she had buried a two-day-old son, Fortunato Crisci, on strada Camellara.
settles: Closed, and now confirmed a second way. The younger Arcangelo, born about 1787, married the line's own Anna Falco, born about 1795; the elder, born about 1765, is Andreana's father. ANDREANA'S BAPTISM, found in her 1814 marriage dossier in September 2026, proves the second half by arithmetic rather than inference: she was baptised on 30 November 1796, so her father was a married man with a child that year — the elder was thirty-one, the younger was NINE. Two men, and both of them married a Falco or fathered a Falco's wife. Note that this archive previously said Anna died «at 22» — the act says TWENTY-FIVE.

q: Sara Ruggiero's death — ANSWERED. She did not die.
known: The last thing standing between this archive and a closed Arcangelo Crisci question. The elder Arcangelo could only ALSO have married Anna Falco if his wife Sara Ruggiero had died between December 1814, when she consented before a notary to her daughter's marriage, and about 1818. The 1815 death register — the only unread year in that window — has now been read end to end: 77 acts, no Sara Ruggiero. And act 4 of 9 January 1815 does better than a negative: «CARMELA CRISCI figlia d'ARCANGELO CRISCI, e SARA RUGGIERO, di giorni sette, domiciliata strada Camellara» — SHE BORE A CHILD IN THE FIRST WEEK OF 1815. A new daughter of the family, Adriana's baby sister, born three weeks after Adriana's wedding and dead at seven days. The declarants are the two families side by side: ANDREA CRISCI, 42, and GIUSEPPE FALCO, 30, both of strada Camellara, both «vicini» — neighbours, and this archive does not upgrade that word.
settles: Closed. TWO Arcangelo Crisci, and Anna Falco married the younger. THE TRAP THIS NEARLY FELL INTO IS WORTH RECORDING: a Sara Ruggiero DID die at Arienzo on 13 December 1817, and she was married to an ARCANGELO. She is a different woman — daughter of the late Raffaele Ruggiero and Fortunata Villano, wife of Arcangelo SOSSI, not Crisci. Two women of one name in one town, both married to an Arcangelo. And the families are linked: Fortunata Villano, that woman's mother, stood godmother at Adriana Crisci's baptism in 1796. Noted, not built on.

q: Chiara Rivetti's age — three answers, none agreeing
known: The banns of September 1814 make her FORTY-SEVEN, implying a birth about 1767. Her burial of 1843 made her EIGHTY, implying 1763. The family tree says 1772. The same 1814 act gets her son's age and her son's bride's age right to the year, so the clerk was not uniformly careless — he was careless about her.
settles: Her baptism, in the Arienzo parish register. Not on Antenati.

q: The Arienzo parish baptism register, liber IX
known: The 1814 marriage dossier quotes it twice — folio 47 a tergo for Vincenzo Falco's baptism of 1792, folio 94 a tergo for Adriana Crisci's of 1796. So in September 1814 the volume was in the hands of the archpriest Giacinto Morgillo at Sant'Andrea Apostolo. IT IS NOT ON ANTENATI. If it survives it holds the baptisms of this entire generation, and it reaches a generation earlier than the civil registers begin in 1809.
settles: Ask the parish of Sant'Andrea and the Museo Alfonsiano at Arienzo. Not attempted.

q: Pasquale Falco's age, off by fourteen
known: The banns call him SIXTY, implying a birth about 1754. His baptism is 24 October 1767, which makes him FORTY-SIX. The same document gets his son and his son's bride right to the year. This is not an open question about who he was — he is documented — but about how much weight any stated age in these registers can carry. It is recorded because this archive publishes the failures of its sources as readily as their successes.
settles: Nothing to search. The baptism stands; the banns age is wrong.

q: Eight people the family graph REFUSES to merge
known: The person graph joins a register household to a tree person only when the name AND a date agree, or when the name is unique on both sides. Where two or more people in the tree share a name and none of them matches a date, IT REFUSES and counts the refusal. Eight names stand refused: ANDREANA CRISCI (2 in the tree), ANGELA FALCO (2), ANGELO FALCO (4), CRESCENZO FALCO (3), FRANCESCO FALCO (4), GIOACCHINO FALCO (2), and two more. These are not bugs. They are the archive's open identity questions, and forcing them would manufacture a genealogy.
settles: Each needs a date from a record. ANDREANA CRISCI is the closest: her baptism is now documented — 30 November 1796 — and it has been added to the tree, but the household side of her record carries only 1818 (her age at her son's birth), so the years still do not overlap and the merge is still refused. It will join the day a record gives her a 1796 event on the register side.

q: Twelve people joined to nobody — one fewer than there was
known: Twelve of the 549 people in this archive have no parent, no spouse, no child and no sibling. They are: Antonio and Giovanni Cioffi (of the Michele Falco household), Giuseppe di Guida, GIOACCHINO FALCO, a Giuseppe Falco, LUCRETIA FALCO, MARGARITA FALCO, MARIA ROSA FALCO, a Matteo Falco (possidente, strada Porta di Sopra), Francesco and Giuseppe QUOTOLO, and Don Giuseppe Rivetti. SILVESTRO QUOTOLO HAS LEFT THIS LIST. The graph was taught on 13 September 2026 to read the register's own prose — 2,768 rows that say «named as a parent of X», 544 that say «named as the spouse of», and a third phrasing that names a child by FORENAME ONLY and appends the household. Silvestro's row is one of those: «named as ANNA's father … Don Nicola Rivetti & Donna Anna Quotolo». A bare forename is not an identification, so it is resolved against that household and nowhere else. He now has his daughter.
settles: 22 edges added and 3,291 REFUSED, under the same rule the rest of this site uses for a name: an edge is made only when both sides answer to exactly one person. The yield is small against 2,768 because most of those rows name people this graph does not hold — it has 429 distinct names against the register's 5,074. THAT, and not an oversight, is why the twelve remain. GIOACCHINO FALCO HAS LEFT THIS LIST TOO. On 13 September 2026 the alphabetical index bound at the front of the Arienzo death register for 1851 was read: «7. FALCO GIOACCHINO | Arienzo | CONTADINO | FALCO MATTEO, e CRISCI FRANCESCA | 14 Febrajo». A record names his parents at last, and he is a documented fifth child of the founding couple. The archive had suspected it since 1816, when he and Giuseppe Falco declared the death of Crescenzo Rivetti as «parenti» — Crescenzo being the husband of their sister Angela. The inference was right, and it is now a document. Eleven people remain joined to nobody.

q: The unnamed child
known: Matteo and Francesca baptised a child that day whose name the transcription does not carry.
settles: The register image.

q: Was Chiara Rivetti gentry? — ANSWERED. No.
known: This was the oldest open question in the archive. Chiara Rivetti married Pasquale Falco of generation two, and the only record that named her parents was a Latin burial entry calling her «filia quondam NICOLAI et ANNA» — two forenames and nothing else. TWO couples of Arienzo answered to them: the gentry DON NICOLA RIVETTI and DONN'ANNA QUOTOLO, both with acts of their own; and the labouring NICOLA RIVETTI, contadino, and ANNA DI RUGGIO, named in the 1821 death act of their son Carmine. The archive weighed them, said the labouring couple was the better fit because Chiara married a contadino and lived among day-labourers on strada Camellara, and then refused to claim it — because a preference is not a record.
settles: THE CIVIL ACT SETTLES IT, and the preference was right. On 13 September 1843, at eight in the evening, «è morta nella sua propria casa CHIARA RIVETTI VEDOVA DI PASQUALE FALCO, nata in Arienzo, di anni OTTANTA, di professione CONTADINA, domiciliata ivi, FIGLIA DI NICOLA RIVETTI DEFUNTO, DI PROFESSIONE CONTADINO, domiciliato ivi, E DI ANNA DI RUGGIO DEFUNTA». The father's trade is written out: a contadino, not a Don. The gentry couple is ruled out. And CARMINE RIVETTI, the man buried in 1821 as a son of the same couple, was Chiara's BROTHER — born about 1768, five years after her. Her death was declared by two Cioffi of strada Camellara.

q: Angela Falco's death of 1829 — PROBABLY SOLVED
rank: Arienzo — parish register vs civil register
known: This archive relied on a parish entry read through machine transcription in which Pasquale Falco is named WITHOUT «quondam» on the death of a daughter ANGELA, dated 1829 — evidence he was then alive. THAT REASONING IS NOW DISPROVED AS A CLASS, not just doubted: on 14 September 2026 the archpriest Giacinto Morgillo was caught writing «filium Matthaei», with no «q.», SEVENTEEN DAYS AFTER he had buried Matteo Falco — while using «filium q. Caroli Antonii» correctly for a dead father four weeks earlier in the same register. But the 1829 civil death register, read image by image, contains no Angela Falco and no Falco of any name. THE 1820 REGISTER NOW OFFERS A BETTER CANDIDATE: on 23 August 1820 ANNA FALCO, twenty-five, died on strada Camellara, and her act names her father Pasquale Falco without «fu» — exactly the shape of the entry the archive was relying on. Anna against Angela, 1820 against 1829: both are the kind of slip a machine transcription makes.
settles: Very likely the same event, misread and misdated. What would settle it: the parish register image for 1820 and for 1829, read directly rather than through the transcription. Either way the point is now moot for the line — Pasquale is independently documented alive in August 1820 and dead on 1 October 1834.

q: The siblings who stayed in Italy
known: Raffaele Falco and Costanza Maione had children at Arienzo besides Carminantonio, who emigrated — Giovanna in 1898 and Gerardo in 1913. Neither has been traced beyond their birth record. Their descendants would be the closest living relatives of this family still in Campania, and nobody has looked for them.
settles: The Arienzo civil registers after 1900, and the Caserta indexes; ordinary research, not a blocked door.

q: The emigrant generation is only half followed
known: Carminantonio's son Raffaele reached Brisbane, married Caterina Zampiello and is buried at Nudgee; his family has not been worked through. Four Zampiello sisters reached Queensland and two married out, into Servodio and Miceli — both surnames are named in the immigration files and then dropped.
settles: The NAA files already identified, and Queensland records.

q: Is the third Maria Falco kin? — ANSWERED
known: A third Maria Falco, wife of FRANCESCO CIOFFI, buried five children on strada Camellara between 1823 and 1828 — Antonia in June 1823, Giuseppe in March 1824, Giuseppa in April 1825, Giuseppe in May 1827, Mariantonia in October 1828. GIUSEPPE FALCO of the same street declared every one of them. This archive read the register as calling him «vicino» — neighbour — every single time, recorded the relationship as NOT ESTABLISHED and refused to join the households, though five turns for one family is a great deal of neighbourliness. **IT DID NOT CALL HIM «VICINO» EVERY TIME. That was a misreading, corrected 16 September 2026.**
settles:
**CLOSED BY THE SECOND ACT, NOT THE FIFTH — AND THIS ENTRY SAID THE FIFTH UNTIL 16 SEPTEMBER 2026.**

The act of **25 March 1824** enters **both** Falco declarants as «*sono comparsi **PASQUALE FALCO** … **ZIO DEL DEFUNTO**, e **GIUSEPPE FALCO** … **ZIO DEL DEFUNTO***» — **uncle**, written twice, over the body of Giuseppe Cioffi, five years old, son of Francesco Cioffi and this Maria Falco. This archive transcribed that word as «vicino». The 1823 and 1825 acts of the same household, in the same hand, **do** write the six-letter «vicino della defunta», and they are the control that proves the three-letter word is not it.

**The 1828 act still says what it said**: «*GIUSEPPE FALCO, di anni cinquantasei, di professione POSSIDENTE, domiciliato in strada CAMELLARA, **PARENTE DELLA DEFUNTA***», with the same word for the second declarant, **Cesare CIOFFI** (this entry said «Cesare Cossi»). **But it is the second statement of kinship, four years later and a weaker word, not the first.**

**THE DEGREE IS STILL UNSTATED IN ONE DIRECTION AND IMPOSSIBLE IN THE OTHER.** «Zio del defunto» read strictly makes Maria Falco a **sister** of Pasquale (baptised 24 October 1767) and Giuseppe, and therefore a **daughter of Matteo Falco and Francesca Crisci**. Her own stated age forbids it: **twenty-five in June 1824**, born about 1799, when Francesca Crisci was bearing children by 1767. Either that age is one of this register's inventions — and the same clerk makes Giuseppe Falco forty and forty-five four days apart — or «zio» is doing the loose collateral work that «parente» does in 1828. **The word is recorded and the pedigree is refused.**

The old caution still travels with the answer: Giuseppe Falco is **fifty-six and a possidente** in 1828 and **forty and a massaro** in April 1825, so whether the man who declared all five acts is one person or two is still not certain.

q: How old is Giuseppe Falco? — the register answers, badly
known: Giuseppe Falco of strada Camellara, a documented son of Matteo Falco, appears seven times as a declarant. His stated age runs 37 (1817), 40 (1825), 46 (1826), 46 (1826), 40 (1827), 56 (1828) and 56 (1843) — and his trade runs massaro di campagna, massaro, massaro, massaro, COLONO, POSSIDENTE, colono. The archive carried this as a straight either-or: one man with careless clerks, or two men on one street.
settles: THE 1843 ACT DECIDES IT, or nearly. The register gives him as FIFTY-SIX in October 1828 and FIFTY-SIX AGAIN in May 1843 — fifteen years apart. No man is the same age fifteen years later, and two different men would not land on the same wrong number. This is what a guess looks like. The archive now leans to ONE Giuseppe Falco, born about 1780, whose age was estimated at the desk by whoever was standing there. It is not proof, and a birth act would settle it; but it is enough to stop treating any single stated age in these volumes as a date.

q: Cossi, Crisci, or Cioffi? — ANSWERED, BOTH HALVES
rank: Arienzo, 1823–1843 — a reading, not a fact
known: PART ONE. The household carried since 1823 as «Francesco COSSI and the third Maria Falco» of strada Camellara — the house whose five dead children Giuseppe Falco declared — is FRANCESCO CIOFFI AND MARIA FALCO. The 1825 volume, read at full resolution, writes the Camellara family with a dotted «i» after the C (Cesare Cioffi, Francesco Cioffi, Giuseppa Cioffi) and, in the same hand and the same book, writes the unrelated family of strada Cossi without one (Domenico Cossi, Crescenzo Cossi). The 1816 volume, in a wholly different hand, writes Cioffi plainly on the same street twelve years earlier. The correction is published, not swapped: the reading logs keep the original text under a banner.
settles: PART TWO IS NOW CLOSED TOO, AND BY ACCIDENT. On 4 December 1827 a priest was buried — «Don Giuseppe C—, cinquantasei, SACERDOTE, figlio di ANDREA —, POSSIDENTE, e di ORSOLA ZIMBARDO» — and no magnification would separate Crisci from Cossi in that hand. On 3 June 1843, sixteen years later and in a different hand, the register buries CELIA CIOFFI, eighty, of strada Porta di Sopra, «figlia di ANDREA CIOFFI defunto, di professione POSSIDENTE, e di ORSOLA ZIMBARDO defunta». Same father, same trade, same mother, spelled plainly. THE PRIEST WAS DON GIUSEPPE CIOFFI, and Celia was his sister. What remains is smaller: the household this archive holds as «Marcello Crisci & Maria Rosa Mauro» from an 1823 act, which the 1828 register writes as «Marcello Cossi» with the identical wife. On the balance of everything above, Cioffi is the likelier third reading — but it has not been seen written, and so it is not claimed.

q: Two daughters called Maria
known: Pasquale and Chiara named a daughter Maria in September 1789 and again in October 1790. Ordinarily that means the first died. No burial has been found.
settles: The Arienzo death register, 1789–90.

q: Is the Gennaro Morgillo who died on 4 August 1843 the father of Crescenzo Falco's wife?
rank: Arienzo processetti 1845 — the dossier behind marriage act 3 of 2 February 1845
known: Four things agree and none of them is a document. The 1843 death act (Morti 1843 act 33, an_ua14345 img24R) gives GENNARO MORGILLO, fifty-three, COLONO of strada Camellara, widower of a FELICIA, son of ANGELO MORGILLO defunto, colono of the Monticello de' Cappuccini. The 1845 marriage gives the bride as «figlia di GENNARO MORGILLO DEFUNTO, di professione colono, e di MARIA FELICIA SANZONE … defunta», living on strada Cappuccini. Forename, surname, trade, the wife's forename, the order of the two deaths and the street all agree. Morgillo is the commonest surname in these registers and this archive already holds two distinct Angelo Morgillo, so agreement is not identity.
settles: The processetto for the 1845 marriage. It must contain Gennaro Morgillo's death certificate, and that certificate carries an act number. If the number is 33 of 1843, the question is closed in one line.

q: Who was Sabbatino Annecchino's paternal grandfather?
rank: Arienzo processetti 1860 — the dossier behind marriage act 3 of 21 January 1860
known: Nothing but that he existed and that his death act was produced. The marriage act of 21 January 1860 lists its eight supporting documents, and the fourth is «Nell'atto di morte dell'AVO PATERNO dello stesso» — the death act of the groom's paternal grandfather, that is the father of CARMINE ANNECCHINO of Forchia. This archive has never named him. It is a generation above the earliest Annecchino it holds.
settles: The processetto itself. A Neapolitan marriage dossier keeps the certified copies, so the act is there with a name, an age, a trade, a street and both of HIS parents.

q: Is Michele Falco's wife ANTONIA VIGLIOTTA or ANTONIA MIGLIORE — or are there two Michele Falco?
rank: Arienzo Morti 1834 act at img24R, against Morti 1842 act 55
known:
On 30 May 1834 a MICHELE FALCO, contadino of Arienzo, buries MARIA ROSA FALCO, twenty-two months old, «figlia di MICHELE FALCO … e di ANTONIA VIGLIOTTA». On 25 August 1842 a MICHELE FALCO, contadino of strada Camellara, buries MATTEO FALCO, two years old, «figlio di MICHELE FALCO … e di ANTONIA MIGLIORE». Same forename, same town, same trade, eight years apart, and the wives share a forename. Neither surname has been magnified against the other.

ANSWERED 20 September 2026: the 1842 word was cropped and set beside the 1834 word in the same hand and they are the same — ANTONIA VIGLIOTTA. «Migliore» was a misreading. The 1850 marriage confirms it from the other end: Michele Falco marries again as «VEDOVO DI ANTONIA VIGLIOTI». The two households are merged. What remains open is a different question — whether this Michele Falco, son of RAFFAELE Falco, is the same man as the MICHELANGELO FALCO son of PASQUALE Falco who married a MARIANTONIA VIGLIOTTA in December 1828. The 1850 act says they had different fathers.
settles: Magnify both surnames at the leaves' full resolution, and read the 1834 act's street. If the two acts give the same street and the surnames are one word misread twice, it is one household; if the streets differ, it is two. A marriage act for either couple would settle it outright.

q: Is there one Raffaela Falco married to a Falco, or two?
rank: Arienzo civil marriages, 1826–1834, and the parish marriage indexes
known: Two acts, fourteen months apart, name a RAFFAELA FALCO as the mother of a dead infant. Arienzo Morti 1832 act 81 (19 December 1832): CARMINA FALCO, six months, «figlia di FRANCESCO FALCO … e di RAFFAELA FALCO». Arienzo Morti 1834 act 16 (16 March 1834): ANNA FALCO, eight days, «figlia di MICHELANGELO FALCO … e di RAFFAELA FALCO». Both fathers are contadini of Arienzo; Michelangelo Falco and Francescantonio Falco are both sons of Pasquale Falco and Chiara Rivetti. Either there are two Raffaela Falco married to two Falco men, or one woman was widowed and remarried inside fourteen months.
settles: A marriage act for either couple. The Arienzo civil marriage registers for 1826–1834 are readable and the parish marriage indexes give both spouses and both sets of parents on one line. A death act for Francesco Falco in 1833 would settle it the other way.

q: Are Michele Falco of Raffaele and Michelangelo Falco of Pasquale the same man?
rank: The Arienzo marriage register for December 1828, and a death act for either Chiara Rivetti
known:
Both married a Vigliotta. MICHELE FALCO, forty-three in February 1850 (b. c. 1807), colono of strada Camellara, is «figlio di RAFFAELE FALCO DEFUNTO … e di CHIARA RIVETTI DEFUNTA, di professione filatrice» and «vedovo di ANTONIA VIGLIOTI». MICHELANGELO FALCO, entered here as a son of PASQUALE FALCO and CHIARA RIVETTI, married MARIANTONIA VIGLIOTTA in December 1828. Two fathers, two wives of one surname, two mothers of one name — and generation two's Chiara Rivetti, widow of Pasquale, died in 1843 aged eighty and cannot have been married to a Raffaele Falco.

20 September 2026, and it moves the balance: the 1836 death act of SALVATORE FALCO, fourteen months, names his parents «MICHELE FALCO … e di MARIANTONIA VIGLIOTTA» — MARIANTONIA, the fuller forename this archive had attached only to the Michelangelo household. So the clerks write her Antonia and Mariantonia indifferently, and the two households now differ in ONE thing only: the husband's forename, Michele against Michelangelo, and a father's name — Raffaele against Pasquale — that comes from a December 1828 record this archive has not re-read from an image.

SHARPENED 20 September 2026 by reading both acts from the image. This archive holds TWO Anna Falco, three years apart, each «figlia di MICHELANGELO FALCO», with two different mothers: Anna of 4 May 1831, thirteen months, «e di MARIANTONIA VIGLIOTTA» (Morti 1831, img20R), and Anna of 16 March 1834, eight days, «e di RAFFAELA FALCO» (Morti 1834, img11L act 16). Both mothers magnified; neither reading is in doubt. A remarriage between the two is excluded if that Mariantonia Vigliotta is the woman still bearing children to a Michele Falco in 1834, 1836 and 1842 whom he survived in 1850. So either there are two Michelangelo Falco at Arienzo, or one of the two mothers belongs to a man of the same name.

ANSWERED 20 September 2026. NO — they are two men. The 1828 marriage index (an_ua14127 img2 act 10) reads «FALCO MICHELANGELO | Arienzo | FALCO PASQUALE, e RIVETTI CHIARA», and the 1850 act's filiation, magnified for the first time, reads «figlio di RAFFAELE FALCO Defunto» with a capital R. Michelangelo is Pasquale's son; Michele is Raffaele's. AND BOTH MARRIED A WOMAN CALLED ANTONIA VIGLIOTTI — Michelangelo's, daughter of Francesco Vigliotti and Vittoria Repetelli, died between May 1831 and March 1834, after which he married RAFFAELA FALCO; Michele's lived until before February 1850. Two women of one name married to two men of almost one name, which is what had the households tangled.
settles: Re-read the December 1828 marriage record from the image. It is the only place the «son of Pasquale Falco» reading comes from, and every other discriminator between the two households has now collapsed.
